catalog_quote: 3.4. TAKIC ACCENTUAL SYSTEMS. Takic accentual systems are diverse. Little is known about secondary stress, so we describe only primary stress. A major distinction among the groups is that in TV and the Serran languages, the domain for stress is the word. ... A short vowel counts as one mora and long vowel as two moras for the placement of stress. In Takic, syllable-final consonants also figure in the mora count ... TV and SE share a system of stress on the syllable containing the second mora of the word, including any prefixes. ... [p. 93] 3.4.1. TONGVA STRESS. In TV, the stress is almost always on the syllable containing the second mora of the word (including prefixes), as seen in (1). ... The examples in (2) show that stress may fall on disyllabic prefixes. ... With a short root, the stress may even fall on what we analyze as a clitic (chapter 8), as in (3). ... [p. 94] In (4) stress falls on the second root syllable in the absolutive form and the first root syllable in the prefixed form. In both examples the stressed syllable contains the second mora. ... A short vowel before another vowel does not count as a mora ... The most common pattern appears to be that stressed vowels will be long, and unstressed vowels will be short. However, a few words with long vowels not marked for stress appear in Harrington’s notes, as in (6) below.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-level primary stress falls on the syllable that contains the second mora counted from the left edge of the whole word (prefixes and reduplicative syllables included): a long vowel counts two moras and a coda consonant adds a mora, so an initial heavy syllable (CVV or CVC) is stressed, otherwise stress goes to the second syllable; a short vowel directly before another vowel does not count. Stressed short vowels lengthen and unstressed vowels reduce to a three-way a/e/o contrast, so stress and length largely coincide.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Sec. 3.4: 'Little is known about secondary stress, so we describe only primary stress.' Sec. 4.2 (c. p.128) speaks of an 'alternating second-mora stress rule' defining strong/weak positions for syncope (the syllable after a stressed long-vowel syllable is strong), but no secondary-stress placement rule is stated for TV.
new_statements.exceptions: 'almost always': disyllabic prefixes may carry the stress alone (ejoo-ken 'our houses') or a long-vowel stem may keep its stress alongside a stressed prefix, and a disyllabic prefix may also surface unstressed (pomo-eehja7); with a short root stress may land on a clitic (ex. 3); a few Harrington forms have unstressed long vowels (omoo-kii-n, ijoo-$uun); kiingáarot 'householder' is stressed on the third-mora syllable (single, possibly forced elicitation); short stressed vowels in open syllables (toruxo7am) are 'quite rare'; the proclitic prohibitive xa= stays unstressed with stress on the following imperative clitic (sec. 8, p. c. 700); clitics are otherwise extrametrical; whether TV has Cupan-style 'stressless roots' 'has yet to be tested' (3.4.9).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word including prefixes and reduplication (contrast Cupan, where prefixes are extrametrical); enclitics/auxiliary clitic complex normally extrametrical. Data are J. P. Harrington's field transcriptions (1910s-30s) of Gabrielino (TVG) and Fernandeño (TVF) speakers, re-spelled in Munro's practical orthography; stress marks are Harrington's.
new_statements.identity_note: Hill & Hill 2019 use 'TV' (Tongva) for the whole language, covering both the Gabrielino/San Gabriel dialect (TVG) and the Fernandeño/San Fernando dialect (TVF; Glottolog also has fern1234 as a separate code in our target list), from J. P. Harrington's notes (principal Gabrielino consultant José de los Santos Juncos and others). The stress statement is given for TV as a whole with no dialect difference noted; it matches Glottolog tong1329 'Tongva' (alt. Gabrielino-Fernandeño), ISO xgf. The language has had no L1 speakers since the mid-20th century; all data are archival.

sources.note: Sec. 3.4 (p.92) and 3.4.1 'Tongva stress' (pp.93-95): TV stress domain is the word; stress falls almost always on the syllable containing the second mora of the word, prefixes included (long V = 2 moras, coda consonants count, prevocalic short V does not count); stressed vowels usually long; a few exceptions (unstressed long vowels, one third-mora form kiingáarot); little known about secondary stress; sec. 4.1.1 (p.121) and 4.2 (c. p.128, 'alternating second-mora stress rule') restate it.

Consonant/vowel inventory (short vs long vowels) after Munro's interpretation of Harrington; nothing on stress. Cites Munro & Gabrielino/Tongva Language Committee 2008 'Lesson One', Golla 2011, McCawley 1996.
